concepts.title: Why can a sound make you expect something?
concepts.definition: Learning an association between stimuli can cause a previously neutral cue to elicit a learned response.
concepts.explanation: A familiar sound may begin to predict an event after repeated pairings.
concepts.example: Your phone's notification sound can create an expectation of a message.

concepts.title: Why do similar cues evoke similar responses?
concepts.definition: A conditioned response can occur to stimuli resembling the learned cue.
concepts.explanation: Generalization allows a learned response to extend beyond one precise stimulus.
concepts.example: A pet responds to several similar food-container sounds.

concepts.title: Can a learned association become weaker?
concepts.definition: A conditioned response weakens when a conditioned cue repeatedly occurs without the expected unconditioned stimulus.
concepts.explanation: Extinction describes a change in responding rather than necessarily erasing the original learning.
concepts.example: The sound that once predicted a snack stops prompting anticipation.

concepts.title: Why can an old response return after a pause?
concepts.definition: An extinguished conditioned response may reappear after a rest period.
concepts.explanation: Extinction does not always permanently remove the prior association.
concepts.example: A cue that seemed unimportant yesterday briefly brings back an old expectation.

concepts.title: How do consequences change our habits?
concepts.definition: Behaviour changes as a function of the consequences that follow it.
concepts.explanation: Reinforcement makes a response more likely; punishment makes it less likely.
concepts.example: Positive feedback following a helpful action may encourage doing it again.

concepts.title: What does positive reinforcement actually mean?
concepts.definition: Adding a consequence after a behaviour increases the likelihood of that behaviour.
concepts.explanation: Positive means an event is added, not necessarily that it feels nice to everyone.
concepts.example: Receiving appreciation after helping may make helping more likely.

concepts.title: Is removing something always punishment?
concepts.definition: Removing an aversive condition after a behaviour increases that behaviour.
concepts.explanation: Negative means removing a condition; reinforcement still increases responding.
concepts.example: Fastening a seat belt stops an irritating reminder, encouraging fastening it.

concepts.title: Does sensing something mean noticing it?
concepts.definition: Sensation detects stimulus energy; perception organizes and interprets sensory information.
concepts.explanation: The same sensory input can be interpreted using experience and context.
concepts.example: Smelling cinnamon is sensation; recognizing a favourite baked food is perception.

concepts.title: Why does a constant smell fade from awareness?
concepts.definition: Sensitivity to an unchanging stimulus often decreases with continuing exposure.
concepts.explanation: This helps explain why some persistent sensations become less noticeable.
concepts.example: After a few minutes in a room, you may hardly notice its scent.

concepts.title: How do expectations shape what you see?
concepts.definition: Perception can be influenced by prior knowledge, goals, and expectations.
concepts.explanation: Interpreting sensory input draws on more than the raw features of the stimulus.
concepts.example: You recognize unclear handwriting more easily when you know the sentence topic.

concepts.title: What happens when you remember a fact?
concepts.definition: Remembering involves encoding information, retaining it, and retrieving it later.
concepts.explanation: These are distinct functions of a memory system.
concepts.example: Studying a definition, keeping it over time, and recalling it in an exam involve these stages.

concepts.title: Remembering an event versus knowing a fact
concepts.definition: Episodic memory concerns personal events, while semantic memory concerns general knowledge and meanings.
concepts.explanation: Both are forms of declarative memory but represent different kinds of content.
concepts.example: Recalling your last birthday differs from knowing what a birthday is.

concepts.title: Why does linking ideas support memory?
concepts.definition: Elaborative rehearsal connects new material with information already known.
concepts.explanation: Meaningful links can improve retention compared with repeating an item without context.
concepts.example: Relating a new research term to a familiar experiment may help you remember it.

concepts.title: Is an emotion just a feeling?
concepts.definition: Emotional experience involves subjective feelings together with expression, appraisal, and physiological changes.
concepts.explanation: The components may influence each other, and their timing can vary.
concepts.example: Feeling nervous before a presentation can involve thoughts, bodily changes, and facial expression.
